statement: In people who had drugs tested at an English festival (2016) or with fentanyl test strips in North America (2016 to 2019), a result showing something unexpected, compared with an expected result, is associated with more people getting rid of drugs, though most did not, and how many depended on the setting. At one English festival, where chemists tested drugs on site and staff gave each result in a consultation, 30 of 45 people whose drug was not what it had been sold as (67 in 100) handed over drugs for police destruction, against 15 of 164 whose drug matched (9 in 100); the service saw these handovers, but people may have kept or thrown away other drugs elsewhere, and 111 of the 164 with a matching result said they would take their usual amount. Among people who use opioids, few said they got rid of a drug after a strip showed fentanyl: at a Vancouver supervised injection site, staff recorded an intention to throw the drug away after 50 of 436 checks before use that showed fentanyl (11 in 100), against 10 of 134 that did not (7 in 100), a difference that may be chance (odds ratio 1.60, 95% CI 0.79 to 3.26), and in a Rhode Island pilot 10 in 100 of 31 young adults with a positive strip said they threw the drugs out. A systematic review of drug checking services to 2019 reports disposal from 0 to 10 in 100 across studies, observed at Canadian festivals at 4 and 7 in 100, and more often after unexpected results; the authors of the Vancouver study link the low rate to dependence, lack of money to replace drugs and no access to unadulterated drugs. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: At one festival where chemists tested drugs, about 2 in 3 people whose drug was not what it had been sold as handed over drugs to be destroyed, against about 1 in 11 whose drug matched. People who use opioids rarely said they would throw a drug away after a strip showed fentanyl: about 1 in 10. Most of these figures are what people said they would do; only the festival handovers were seen by staff.
population: People who had drugs tested: clients of an on-site festival testing service in England (230 consultations, 2016); checks before use at a Vancouver supervised injection site (2016–17); young adults with a positive strip result in a Rhode Island pilot (2017); studies of drug checking services in one systematic review (to October 2019)
exposure: A result showing something unexpected: a drug not as sold (festival) or fentanyl detected (strips)
comparator: A result matching what was sold (festival) or not showing fentanyl (Vancouver)
outcome: Handing over drugs for destruction (observed, festival), stated intention to throw the drug away (Vancouver), self-reported throwing out (Rhode Island), and disposal rates relayed by a review
magnitude: Festival (observed): 30/45 (66.7%; Wilson 52.1–78.6%) against 15/164 (9.1%; 5.6–14.5%), p < .01; difference 57.5 points (Newcombe 42.0–70.0), risk ratio 7.3 (editors' calculations); 49/230 (21.3%) overall; stated intention to take the usual amount 111/164 (67.7%) with a matching result against 4/45 (8.9%) with a non-matching one. Vancouver (stated, before use): 50/436 (11.5%) against 10/134 (7.5%), OR 1.60 (0.79–3.26); risk difference 4.0 points (−2.3 to 8.7, editors' calculation). Rhode Island (self-report, n = 31): threw out 10%, sold 10%, gave away 7%. Review (relayed): 0–10% across studies; observed 4% (n = 2078) and 7% (n = 2786) at Canadian festivals.

evidence.extracted: Four days at a 25,000-capacity festival in England in July 2016: chemists in an on-site laboratory analysed 247 submitted substances (FTIR, colour reagent tests, mass-loss analysis); results were given in 230 brief consultations with healthcare staff lasting about 15 to 20 minutes, with harm-reduction advice and an offer to hand over further substances for police destruction.

evidence.locator: Results › Individual behavioural outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: 49 of 230 clients (21.3%) handed over further substances for police destruction after hearing their result: 30 of 45 (66.7%) whose sample did not match what it was sold as, against 15 of 164 (9.1%) whose sample matched (p < .01), and 4 of 21 (19%) with samples of unknown origin. Editors' calculation: 66.7% (Wilson 95% CI 52.1–78.6%) against 9.1% (5.6–14.5%), difference 57.5 percentage points (Newcombe 42.0–70.0).

evidence.locator: Results › Individual behavioural outcomes, 2nd paragraph; Table 3
evidence.extracted: Stated intentions from an open-ended question coded afterwards (one per client): take my usual amount 121 of 230, including 111 of 164 (67.7%) with a matching result and 4 of 45 (8.9%) with a non-matching one; throw it away myself 6 (2.6%); take it later or over a longer time 22; take a smaller amount 7; no answer 19 (8.3%). The author notes that some festival-goers may keep their other supplies in their tent and discard unwanted drugs in any nearby bin.

evidence.locator: Controversies in drug safety testing, 4th and 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The author ranks actual disposal immediately after hearing a result as the strongest of four behavioural indicators (against intentions after results, recalled behaviour and hypothetical intentions), and cites a review (Leece, 2017) estimating disposal rates from 4 to 76% across evaluations.

evidence.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, lower panel; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Before use, a stated intention to dispose of the drug followed 50 of 436 fentanyl-positive checks (11.5%) and 10 of 134 negative checks (7.5%), OR 1.60 (95% CI 0.79–3.26). The authors attribute the low rate to dependence on the drugs, lack of money to replace them and no access to unadulterated drugs, and contrast a 2015 festival service where 13% disposed of drugs after an unexpected result and 2% after an expected one. Editors' calculation (card): risk difference 4.0 percentage points (Newcombe 95% CI −2.3 to 8.7).

evidence.extracted: Of the 31 who reported a positive strip result, 10% threw their drugs out, 10% sold them and 7% gave them away (self-reported at follow-up).

evidence.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 5th paragraph; Results › Outcomes related to models of DCS, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Disposal was observed in 5 studies and self-reported in 3, and was more frequent when results were unexpected: observed disposal at Canadian festivals ranged from 4% (n = 2078, 2015) to 7% (n = 2786, 2014); 10% of young adults in the United States disposed of the drug when fentanyl was detected (n = 81, 2017; the Rhode Island pilot); 0% of people who inject drugs did so in another US study (n = 125, 2017); in Canadian qualitative work (n = 20), people using opioids were less likely than people using stimulants to intend disposal if fentanyl was found. The review cites a UK festival (n = 230, 2016), the festival of Measham (2019), for clients' reasons for testing.
evidence.located_by: AI reader 140 (first reader), from AI reader 137's study card

risk_of_bias.note: Festival: self-selected clients, many already worried about their sample, one primary client per group and no follow-up (ROBINS-I critical for effects; the handovers themselves were observed). Vancouver: intentions recorded by staff and not followed. All comparisons by result are unadjusted.

inconsistency.note: The size differs greatly (67 in 100 at the festival, about 10 in 100 among people who use opioids), in line with the setting: festival-goers whose drug was not as sold against people who use opioids, for whom fentanyl was common and often expected; the direction is the same.

indirectness.note: The clearest data come from one festival in 2016 where chemists tested drugs and staff gave a consultation, not from kits used at home; the strip data are intentions and self-reports.

imprecision.note: The festival difference is large relative to its interval (42 to 70 points); the Vancouver difference is imprecise (−2 to 9 points) and is reported as such.

grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; risk of bias and indirectness each take a level: very low. Worded as an association between the result and getting rid of drugs, not as an effect of testing (there is no group without testing). Counted once: Krieger et al. is the review's '10% of young adults', and the review cites the same festival (n = 230, 2016) for clients' reasons for testing, so the festival and the review overlap. Status replicated: the festival and the Vancouver site, independent studies, point the same way, as does the review's summary, though the Vancouver difference is imprecise.
